13.01.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this spinal implant?"
- "Spinal instrumentation = **anchors** joined by **longitudinal members**."
- "Anchors are screws, hooks or wires; members are rods or plates; cages prop the front."

| Implant | Look for | Where |
|---|---|---|
| **Pedicle screw + rod** | tulip head, rod, set screw | thoracolumbar spine |
| **Lateral mass screw** | short screws, thin rods | C3–C6 |
| **Interbody cage** | box in disc space, markers | any disc level |
| **Anterior cervical plate** | low plate, short screws | front of the neck |
| **Odontoid screw** | one screw up the dens | C2 |
| **Hooks, sublaminar wires** | under the lamina | old scoliosis constructs |
| **Vertebroplasty cement** | white cloud in a body | osteoporotic fracture |

- A pedicle screw grips all three columns: the strongest posterior anchor
- Posterior screws and rods are a **tension band**; a cage in front carries compression

- Posterior screws and rods with a TLIF cage at L4–L5
- Anterior cervical cage, alone and with a plate

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Anchor it, link it, prop the front**

13.02.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this screw?"
- "A **pedicle screw**: head (tulip), shank with cancellous thread, blunt tip."
- "It passes through the pedicle into the body; a rod locks in its head."

### Parts
| Part | Job |
|---|---|
| **Head (tulip)** | U-shaped saddle, takes the rod |
| **Set screw** (locking cap) | locks the rod in the head |
| **Shank** | deep cancellous thread |
| **Tip** | blunt or self-tapping |

- Material: titanium alloy → less artefact on CT and MRI after surgery

- Polyaxial tulip-head screw with its set screw

### Types (Nagah)
| Type | Head | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Monoaxial** (fixed) | one piece with shank | derotation, fracture reduction |
| **Polyaxial** | swivels in a cone | easy rod seating |
| **Uniplanar** | moves in one plane | rod seating plus derotation |

- Polyaxial head swings about **20–25°** from the screw axis (Nagah)
- Fixed heads derotate best; use polyaxial screws only if needed (Campbell)

- Side-loaded: rod beside the screw (old); top-loaded: rod drops into the head

- Fixed, polyaxial and uniplanar screws with their motion

### Special screws
- **Cannulated**: passes over a guide wire, for percutaneous fixation
- **Fenestrated**: side holes for cement → more pull-out strength in osteoporosis
- Newer options: expandable screws for osteoporosis, coated screws against infection, navigation

- Fenestrated cannulated screw for cement augmentation

### Sizes — the pedicle decides
| Level (Nagah) | Pedicle width |
|---|---|
| T1 | 7 mm |
| T5 | **5 mm** |
| T12 | 7 mm |
| L5 | **17 mm** |

- Narrowest pedicles **T4–T6**, widest at L5 (Campbell)
- Use the widest screw the pedicle accepts
- The medial pedicle wall is about twice as thick as the lateral wall
- Pedicle type D (of A–D) has no channel → juxtapedicular screw (Campbell)

- Pedicle dimensions at T3, T8 and L4

### Uses
| Problem | What the screw does |
|---|---|
| Fracture | fixation, ligamentotaxis |
| Scoliosis, kyphosis | correction |
| Degenerative disease | fusion |
| Tumour, infection | stability after resection |

13.03.t: 13.3 Inserting a Pedicle Screw — Instruments in Order
13.03.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you insert it?"
- "Entry point, awl, pedicle finder, probe, tap, probe again, then the screw."
- "Then image in two planes."

### Entry point
- **Lumbar**: lateral edge of the superior facet meets the mid-line of the transverse process
- That corner is the **mammillary process**
- **Thoracic**: a few millimetres below and lateral to the facet–transverse process junction

- Lumbar entry points: Roy-Camille and Weinstein
- Entry where facet line meets transverse process line

### Trajectory
| Lumbar level (Handbook) | Medial angle |
|---|---|
| L1 | 5° |
| L3 | 15° |
| L5 | 25° |
| S1 | 30° |

- Sagittal tilt: upward at L1–L2, neutral at L3–L4, downward at L5–S1
- A medial aim gives a longer screw, spares the facet and keeps off the iliac vessels

### The instruments (Handbook; Campbell)
1) **Burr or rongeur** (nibbler) opens the cortex at the entry
2) **Awl**: a sharp tip that perforates the cortex
3) **Pedicle finder** (gearshift probe, "makhraz"): blunt, tapered tip
4) It pushes cancellous bone aside to make the track; it does not cut

5) In the thoracic spine, point the tip lateral for the first **20–25 mm**
6) Then turn it medial and advance to the planned depth
7) Adolescent depth, low thoracic: about **30–40 mm** (Campbell)
8) Mid and upper thoracic: about **20–30 mm**

9) **Ball-tipped probe** (feeler): feel the floor and four walls
10) Feel the first 10–15 mm hardest: that depth lies beside the canal
11) **Tap**: undertap by **0.5–1 mm** of the screw diameter
12) Feel the walls again; then insert the screw

- Thoracic pedicle screw steps: finder, probe, tap
- Ball-tipped sounder checking the track

### Checks
- Sudden give, or clear fluid from the track → breach
- Freehand screws: **5–15%** malpositioned; navigation lowers it (Campbell)
- A **30°** oblique "near-approach" view shows an anterior breach better than a lateral (Campbell)
- Percutaneous screws: Jamshidi needle, guide wire, then cannulated tap and screw through stab incisions

- Percutaneous pedicle screw steps

| Breach (Nagah) | Hits |
|---|---|
| Medial | dura, cord |
| Inferior | nerve root |
| Anterior | aorta, great vessels |

PITFALL — "which wall is the dangerous one?"
- The medial wall is thick, but breaching it reaches the dura
- Say → "**Aim lateral first. Medial and inferior breaches hit the dura and the root.**"

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Open, push, feel, tap, feel, screw**

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what holds the screws together?"
- "A **rod** in each screw head, locked by a **set screw**."
- "A **cross-link** may join the two rods."

### Rods
- Rods are titanium, stainless steel or cobalt-chrome
- Cobalt-chrome is stiffest → better hold of the correction in deformity surgery
- Bend it with a French bender; repeated bending notches it → later breakage

### Set screw and reduction
- Final tightening: torque wrench plus **counter-torque**, so the screw does not twist
- Compressing or distracting along the rod, before final tightening, corrects the segment

### Cross-link (transverse connector)
- It joins the rods → torsional stiffness; often unneeded with modern screws

- Screw–rod construct with a cross-link on X-ray and CT

13.05.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "which screw at which cervical level?"
- "**C3–C6**: lateral mass screws. **C2**: pedicle, pars or translaminar."
- "**C1**: lateral mass screw (Harms). Pedicle screws are safe mainly at C2 and C7."

### Why not pedicle screws everywhere?
- Cervical pedicles are narrow, except at C2 and C7
- The vertebral artery runs in the foramen transversarium, just lateral to the pedicle
- **C2**: large pedicle; the foramen lies far lateral
- **C7**: the artery usually does not enter its foramen (Nagah)

| | Pedicle screw | Lateral mass screw |
|---|---|---|
| Grip | strong, into the body | weaker, cancellous bone |
| Risk | artery, cord | root, artery if medial |
| Used at | C2, C7 | C3–C6 |

- C7 pedicle screw beside a lateral mass screw

### Lateral mass screw
- Entry: about **1 mm** medial to the centre of the lateral mass (Campbell)

| Technique | Lateral aim | Upward aim |
|---|---|---|
| **Roy-Camille** | 10° | none |
| **Magerl** | 25° | parallel to facet |
| **An** | 30° | 15° |

- Rest the drill guide on the spinous process of the level below → the right angle
- Screw: **3.5 mm** wide (Kim)
- Length: **14 mm** unicortical is enough

- Lateral mass landmarks and drill angle
- Lateral mass entry point and trajectory
- Lateral mass screws and rods from C3 to C7

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Roy ten, Magerl twenty-five, An thirty**

### C2 screws — the Nagah question
| C2 pedicle screw (Nagah; Campbell) | Value |
|---|---|
| Diameter | **3.5 mm** |
| Medial aim | **25°** |
| Upward aim | **20–30°** |
| Stops | before the foramen transversarium |

- Entry: upper, medial part of the C2 isthmus; see its medial wall first (Kim)

- **Pars screw**: follows the pars, steeper and shorter; it stops behind the artery
- **Translaminar screws**: two crossing screws inside the C2 laminae
- Use them when the artery rides high: about **20%** of people (Campbell)

| C2 translaminar (Kim) | Value |
|---|---|
| Lamina thickness | about **5.8 mm** |
| Lamina length | about **25 mm** |
| Screw diameter | **3.5–4.0 mm** |
| Screw length | **20–30 mm** |

- C2 pars screw: medial and upward angles
- Crossing C2 translaminar screws

### C1–C2 and the occiput
- **Harms**: C1 lateral mass screws + C2 pedicle screws, joined by rods
- C1 screw: below the C1 arch, **10°** medial, smooth upper shank
- Ponticulus posticus: a bony bridge over the vertebral artery on C1
- Look for it on CT before a C1 screw (Campbell)

- **Magerl**: one screw crosses the C1–C2 facet joint from C2
- Magerl screw: **3.5–4.0 mm** wide (Kim)
- Its length: **34–44 mm**
- Anatomy rules it out in up to **23%** (Campbell)

- **Occipital plate**: midline, screws below the inion, in an inverted-triangle safe zone

- Harms construct: C1 lateral mass and C2 screws
- Ideal C1 and C2 screw positions on X-ray
- C1–C2 screw–rod fixation on lateral X-rays
- Occipital screw safe zone
- Occipitocervical plate–rod fusion

PITFALL — "Harms or Magerl?"
- Both fix C1 to C2; the screws differ
- Say → "**Harms: separate C1 and C2 screws joined by rods. Magerl: one screw across the joint.**"

13.06.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this anterior neck implant?"
- "**ACDF** (anterior cervical discectomy and fusion): disc out, cage in, plate on the front."
- "A disc prosthesis keeps motion instead of fusing."

### ACDF cage and plate
- Cage: PEEK or titanium, filled with graft, sized to the disc height
- Plate: low profile, with a lock against screw back-out
- Screws are unicortical, usually **14 mm** (Campbell)
- Pick the shortest plate: a long plate irritates the next disc

- **Static** plate holds the graft height; **dynamic** plate lets the graft settle (Li 2023)
- **Zero-profile** cage: screws through the cage, no plate → less swallowing trouble (Zhang 2022)

- Anterior cervical plate: screw angles and lock

### Corpectomy cage
- Vertebral body removed: a mesh or expandable cage spans the gap between endplates
- The defect is at least **17 mm** wide
- A plate is added; screws do not enter the cage

- Expandable cage after cervical corpectomy, with a plate
- Mesh and expandable cages for vertebral body replacement

### Cervical disc arthroplasty
- Two metal endplates and a core: motion kept, the next level spared
- Not for posterior compression, facet arthrosis or instability
- Problems: heterotopic ossification, migration, and subsidence if the disc is undersized

- Cervical disc prosthesis: endplates and core
- Ideal and undersized disc prosthesis positions

### Odontoid screw
- A cannulated **3.5 mm** lag screw from the front of C2
- Entry: anteroinferior edge of C2; aim just behind the dens tip
- First lay a K-wire along the neck to check the path (Campbell)
- A barrel chest can block the steep path (Kim)

- Reduction must be anatomic before the wire goes in
- Avoid it in reverse oblique fractures, comminution and osteoporosis

- Odontoid screw under two image intensifiers
- Type II odontoid fracture before and after screw

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this box in the disc space?"
- "An **interbody cage**: it holds the disc height and carries graft."
- "I name it by the route: PLIF, TLIF, ALIF or lateral."

| Cage (Handbook) | Route | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **PLIF** | through the canal | both sides, retract dura |
| **TLIF** | through the foramen | one side, after facetectomy |
| **ALIF** | from the front | largest cage, best lordosis |
| **XLIF / OLIF** | lateral or oblique | wide cage, no canal |

### Material
- **PEEK**: radiolucent, stiffness near bone; small metal markers show its place
- **Titanium**: bone grows onto it; stiffer → more subsidence; often 3D-printed porous
- **Expandable**: goes in small, opens in place → less endplate damage

- Titanium and PEEK cages for each route
- Expandable lumbar interbody cages

### What each route risks
- Lateral transpsoas: lumbar plexus, thigh numbness, psoas weakness
- ALIF: great vessels; lower rod fracture rate than TLIF
- PLIF and TLIF: dural tear and root injury from retracting them

- Lateral cage above an old fusion

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Back, side door, front, flank: PLIF, TLIF, ALIF, XLIF**

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this old scoliosis rod?"
- "A **Harrington rod**: one distraction rod on hooks."
- "Modern constructs use pedicle screws at many levels instead."

### Generations
| Construct | Anchor | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| **Harrington** | hooks at the ends | flat back, hook dislodgement |
| **Luque** | sublaminar wires, L-rods | wires pass in the canal |
| **Cotrel–Dubousset** | multiple hooks, derotation | hooks sit in the canal |
| **All pedicle screws** | screws at many levels | cost, radiation |

- Sublaminar wiring carries a high risk of cord injury
- Pedicle screws correct curves better than hooks do

- Harrington distraction rod with hooks
- Sublaminar wire construct for scoliosis

### Growing rods
- Early-onset scoliosis: traditional rods are lengthened by repeated surgery
- **Magnetically controlled** rods spare a return to theatre for each lengthening (Campbell)
- Problems on explanted rods: loss of distraction, stud fracture, thread wear (Cheung 2021)

- Dual magnetically controlled growing rods
- Explanted magnetic rods beside their X-ray

### Vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty
- **Vertebroplasty**: bone cement injected straight into the body through a trocar in the pedicle
- **Kyphoplasty**: a balloon makes a cavity first → thicker cement, lower pressure, fewer leaks (Kim)
- Leak into the canal or the veins → cord compression or cement embolism to the lungs

- Balloon kyphoplasty kit: balloon, cannula, gauge
- Vertebroplasty cement with a venous leak

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what is this instrument?"
- "A **Kerrison rongeur**: its footplate goes under the bone, then it bites upward."
- "The **pituitary rongeur** only grasps and pulls disc material."

| Instrument | Look | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Kerrison rongeur** | footplate, upward bite | lamina, ligamentum flavum |
| **Pituitary rongeur** | long shaft, cup jaws | disc nucleus |
| **Leksell rongeur** | double action, big jaws | spinous process, graft |
| **Penfield dissector** | flat, blunt | free the dura |
| **Root retractor** | blunt, L-shaped | protect root and dura |
| **Curette** | angled cup | disc, endplates |
| **High-speed burr** | diamond tip near dura | thin the lamina |

- Keep the dura off the footplate before each bite → no dural tear
- Kerrison is used in laminectomy, laminotomy and microdiscectomy fenestration

- Never push the pituitary through the front annulus: the aorta and iliac vessels lie there

- Kerrison rongeur removing ligamentum flavum
- Pituitary and Kerrison rongeurs clearing the disc space
- Pituitary rongeur with its broken tip

PITFALL — "is the punch a different instrument?"
- Handbook calls the Kerrison a "punch" when it removes disc
- Say → "**Kerrison punch bites bone and flavum. Disc comes out with the pituitary rongeur.**"

13.10.b:
MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what has gone wrong here?"
- "I check each screw, then the rods, the cage, and the level above."

### Malposition
- Graded on axial CT by how many millimetres the screw leaves the pedicle

| Gertzbein–Robbins | Breach |
|---|---|
| Grade 0 | none |
| Grade 1 | under 2 mm |
| Grade 2 | 2–4 mm |
| Grade 3 | over 4 mm |

- Most malpositioned screws cause no symptoms
- Remove or redirect it early if it touches the aorta or a root

- Axial CT grades of pedicle breach

### Loosening and breakage
- **Halo**: a lucent rim around the screw = loosening, common in osteoporosis
- **Rod or screw breakage** usually means **pseudarthrosis**
- Breaks cluster at the lumbosacral junction, at osteotomies and at notched rods

- Lucent halo around a loose pedicle screw on CT
- Broken rods at the lumbosacral junction
- Broken distal pedicle screws

### Cage and the next level
- Cage **subsidence** into the endplate, or **migration** back towards the canal
- **Adjacent segment disease**: the level next to a fusion degenerates
- **Proximal junctional kyphosis**: the top of a long construct folds forward

- TLIF cage subsidence at one year
- Slip at the level above a lumbar fusion

HIGH YIELD — Memory line
- **Halo loose, broken means not fused, sinking cage, look above**
